conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because you were vomiting blood. Can you tell me what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, earlier today I threw up—like, a lot. And there was blood, even clots. I’ve never done that before. I’ve been having stomach pain too, and now chest pain on the left side, goes down my arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Were you drinking today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Had a few beers around 1:30, but I quit drinking two weeks ago. At least I was trying to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, your blood alcohol level is still high. We’re concerned about bleeding in your upper GI tract. We’ll run some tests and likely do an endoscopy tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Endoscopy? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A small camera goes down your throat to look at your stomach and esophagus. We need to find where the bleeding is coming from.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. That sounds rough. But yeah, okay. I’ve had rectal bleeding before, but not this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Your blood count is low—your hemoglobin is 7.6, which is quite low. You’ll likely get a blood transfusion tonight to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had transfusions before. Last time was for anemia. Is this the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but this time it’s likely from acute bleeding. We’ll figure it out. We also did a chest X-ray. There’s a small spot on your lung we want to follow up on later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lung spot? Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s too early to say. It could be nothing, or an old infection. We’ll repeat the X-ray in a few weeks to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood count improved after the transfusion. We’re sending you for an endoscopy this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any idea what they’ll find?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your vomiting and blood, we suspect a small tear in your esophagus—called a Mallory-Weiss tear. But we also need to check for ulcers or varices, which are swollen veins in the esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Varices? I’ve heard that before. Is that from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, often from long-term alcohol use. We’re concerned you might have cirrhosis. We’ll do an ultrasound to check your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy is done. You have mild gastritis—irritation in your stomach—and small grade I varices. No active bleeding was seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no bleeding now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No active bleed, but the tear might have already healed. That’s likely what caused the vomiting of blood. We also found irritation in your stomach, which could be from alcohol or reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So I’m okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not out of the woods yet. You still have low blood counts, and we need to check your colon too. You’ve had rectal bleeding—so we’ll do a colonoscopy tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver ultrasound shows signs of cirrhosis—mild scarring, fluid around the liver, and an enlarged spleen. This supports that you have chronic liver disease, likely from alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cirrhosis? That’s serious, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we can manage it. We’re starting you on a medication called nadolol to reduce pressure in your liver veins and lower the risk of future bleeding from varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on atenolol for blood pressure. Is this different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nadolol is similar but better for liver disease. We’re switching you and increasing the dose gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy is done. You have grade 3 internal hemorrhoids and some small abnormal blood vessels in your colon—called angioectasias. One was clipped to stop potential bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I’ve been bleeding from the back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. The clipped vessel should help, but if bleeding continues, you might need another procedure later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. More scopes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also starting you on iron and vitamin C to help rebuild your blood. And a strong stomach medicine—omeprazole—to help your esophagus and stomach heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve mentioned shortness of breath when walking. We did another chest X-ray. There’s a new shadow in your right lung—likely a mild pneumonia, possibly from inhaling stomach contents during vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I don’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not all pneumonia causes fever, especially in people with liver disease. We’re adding an antibiotic—levofloxacin—for a week to cover it and prevent infection in your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a diuretic—Lasix—to help with fluid. Your blood pressure has been high too, so we started lisinopril. Your heart echo was okay, but you have thickening from long-term high BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. No more vomiting, your blood count is stable, and your breathing has improved. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Discharge? But I still feel tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body is recovering from blood loss and liver strain. But you’re stable. We’ll give you a list of medications and follow-up steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Omeprazole twice daily, nadolol, lisinopril, Lasix, iron with vitamin C, thiamine, and a multivitamin. And the antibiotic for five more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. I might forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over it again before you leave. You’ll also need to see a liver specialist, get vaccines for hepatitis A and B, and repeat a chest X-ray in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t know if I can keep up with all this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But it’s important—especially stopping alcohol, taking your meds, and following up. Your liver can stabilize if you make changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. The nurse will review your medications and instructions. You’re doing well and can go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I think I’ll just go now. I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like you to stay for the full discharge process—medication review, paperwork, and confirming your follow-up. It’s important for your safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get it, but I’m leaving now. I’ll figure it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please reconsider. Without the full plan, you’re at risk for more bleeding, infection, or liver complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been through this before. I’ll be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll document that you’re leaving against medical advice. We’ll try to reach you later to go over the plan. Please take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse, the patient has left the hospital against medical advice. Please document the discharge instructions were not fully reviewed and medications not dispensed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work, can you try to contact the patient later today? We need to ensure he understands the follow-up for cirrhosis, the lung nodule, and his medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI team, patient eloped this morning before formal discharge. He agreed to the plan earlier but left AMA. We’ll need to coordinate outpatient follow-up if he returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pharmacy, please hold discharge meds. Patient did not collect prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll document the hospital course and discharge summary, noting the patient left against advice despite stabilization and a clear recovery plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did everything we could. Now it’s up to him to follow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s flag his record for outreach. He needs hepatology, repeat imaging, and support for alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, ensure the primary care team is notified. This is a high-risk patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And schedule a follow-up chest X-ray reminder for four weeks out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll finalize the discharge summary now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Done. We’ve done our part.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s hope he comes back for care.
